title: Documents key to LRBA grandfathering
full_text:
The number and type of documents that support the acquisition of a residential property via a limited recourse borrowing arrangement (LRBA) that commenced before 10 August but is incomplete will be critical in allowing the grandfathering of it, DBA Lawyers principal Dan Butler has noted.
Butler said while there has been updated guidance for what property can be purchased via an LRBA after 10 August, there was still some uncertainty about arrangements put in place in the weeks leading up to the changes that commenced after that date.
“There is a lot of concern as to what is the test to get in there before 10 August as apparently there was a rush to buy residential property, and the ATO recently put out a release saying there are up to 13,000 funds it might need to check that have reported a property acquisition before 10 August,” he told attendees at the recent Tax Institute National Superannuation Conference in Melbourne.
“If your clients have done this, it’s probably worthwhile checking they do satisfy the criteria and what the ATO focuses on is the exchange of contracts, that is, you do have a a binding contract to acquire real estate, even if settlement takes place at a later date.”
He noted ATO guidance stated this applies to off-the-plan apartments and buildings, as well as existing property, but there were a range of documents also required by different states that could impact whether a residential property LRBA set up before 10 August could be executed in the future.
“The question is what do you need under the belt as of 10 August to gain that grandfathering relief in respect of residential property?” he said.
“A lot of people may not have set up the bare trust, may not have the borrowing approved, particularly for off-the-plan developments, because for some developers it’s not until you get close to completion that the financier will actually consider lending.
“There’s still not a lot of clear criteria for off-the-plan arrangements, but if they’ve got a binding contract, that’s a starting point to build up from there.
“Also, [it would be useful] if they have the bare trust in place in some jurisdictions you need at the time of the acquisition and then the financing.
“It appears it would be good to at least have had some discussions with the financier and it probably will be done [in terms of grandfathering].”
author: Jason Spits
